items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to find the area of the region bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r = 3\cos\theta] and the rays [MATH: \theta_1 = 0] and [MATH: \theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},] as shown in blue in the picture below. Can we calculate this area using polar coordinates?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/0ae57c37a8bcd46584a48b6258ff7d47]

Content:
In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve [MATH: r=r(\theta)] and the rays [MATH: \theta=\theta_1] and [MATH: \theta=\theta_2] is given by the formula

Content:
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta.]

Content:
Therefore, the area of the half-circle above can be obtained as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/2}(3\cos θ)^{2}dθ; = (9)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/2}\cos^{2} θdθ; = (9)/(2)∫_{0}^{π/2}(1)/(2)(1 + \cos (2θ))dθ; = (9)/(4)(θ|_{0}^{π/2} + (1)/(2)\sin (2θ)|_{0}^{π/2}); = (9)/(4)((π)/(2) + 0); = (9π)/(8)]

items.title: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose

sections.normalized_html: Find the area bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r = \cos(3\theta)] and the lines [MATH: \theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}] and [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.]
sections.readable_text:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r = \cos(3\theta)] and the lines [MATH: \theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}] and [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.]

[IMG: /graphics/bb7cc7dd162b6f0a389d6dc6e05c9319]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by [MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.]

When [MATH: r(\theta) = \cos(3\theta),] [MATH: \theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},] and [MATH: \theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6},] this gives

[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{− π/6}^{π/6}\cos^{2} (3θ)dθ; = (1)/(4)∫_{− π/6}^{π/6}(1 + \cos (6θ))dθ; = (1)/(4)(θ|_{− π/6}^{π/6} + (1)/(6)\sin (6θ)|_{− π/6}^{π/6}); = (1)/(4)(((π)/(6) − (− (π)/(6))) + (1)/(6)(\sin π − \sin (− π))); = (1)/(4)((π)/(3) + 0); = (π)/(12).]

sections.readable_text:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r = 1+2\cos\theta] for [MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3},] as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/6471920e9e3f1a0eef69f5be705a6e6c]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by [MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.]

When [MATH: r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),] [MATH: \theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},] and [MATH: \theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},] this gives

[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{2π/3}^{4π/3}(1 + 2\cos (θ))^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{2π/3}^{4π/3}(1 + 4\cos θ + 4\cos^{2} θ)dθ; = (1)/(2)(θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + 4\sin θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + 4 ⋅ (1)/(2)∫_{2π/3}^{4π/3}(1 + \cos (2θ))dθ); = (1)/(2)(θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + 4\sin θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + 2θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + \sin (2θ)|_{2π/3}^{4π/3}); = (1)/(2)(3θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + 4\sin θ|_{2π/3}^{4π/3} + \sin (2θ)|_{2π/3}^{4π/3}); = (1)/(2)(2π − 4sqrt(3) + sqrt(3)); = (1)/(2)(2π − 3sqrt(3)).]

sections.normalized_html: Find the area bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta] for [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},] as shown above.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/0cf3efb2050d3ceed8f1d4dba42a466e]

Find the area bounded by the polar curve [MATH: r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta] for [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},] as shown above.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by [MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.]

When [MATH: r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,] [MATH: \theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] and [MATH: \theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},] this gives

[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(2\sin θ + 2\cos θ)^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(4\sin^{2} θ + 8\sin θ\cos θ + 4\cos^{2} θ)dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(4 + 8\sin θ\cos θ)dθ; = (4)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(1 + \sin (2θ))dθ; = 2(θ|_{π/2}^{3π/4} − (\cos (2θ))/(2)|_{π/2}^{3π/4}); = 2θ|_{π/2}^{3π/4} − \cos (2θ)|_{π/2}^{3π/4}; = 2((3π)/(4) − (π)/(2)) − (\cos ((3π)/(2)) − \cos (π)); = (π)/(2) − 1; = (π − 2)/(2).]

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

When [MATH: r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,] [MATH: \theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] and [MATH: \theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},] this gives

[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(2\sin θ + 2\cos θ)^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(4\sin^{2} θ + 8\sin θ\cos θ + 4\cos^{2} θ)dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(4 + 8\sin θ\cos θ)dθ; = (4)/(2)∫_{π/2}^{3π/4}(1 + \sin (2θ))dθ; = 2(θ|_{π/2}^{3π/4} − (\cos (2θ))/(2)|_{π/2}^{3π/4}); = 2θ|_{π/2}^{3π/4} − \cos (2θ)|_{π/2}^{3π/4}; = 2((3π)/(4) − (π)/(2)) − (\cos ((3π)/(2)) − \cos (π)); = (π)/(2) − 1; = (π − 2)/(2).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We've been using the following formula for the area of the region bounded by a polar curve [MATH: r=r(\theta)] and the rays [MATH: \theta=\theta_1] and [MATH: \theta=\theta_2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta]

Content:
But where does this formula come from?

Content:
To see where the formula comes from, we can think about breaking up the area bounded by a polar curve into infinitesimally small sectors of circles.

Content:
As shown in the graph below, each sector has a radius of [MATH: r] and spans an infinitesimally small angle, [MATH: \textrm d \theta.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f54818e0e1def6c498e34fd18ddf6925]

Content:
The ratio of the area of a sector to the full area of the circle must be the same as the ratio of the angle of the sector to a full revolution of the circle. So, if the area of a sector is [MATH: \textrm dA,] then we can set up and solve the following proportion:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\pi r^2} = \dfrac{\textrm d\theta}{2\pi} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \textrm dA = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \textrm d\theta]

Content:
Finally, to find the area under the curve, we can integrate the areas of all the sectors:

Content:
[MATH: A|= ∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}(1)/(2)r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ]

[MATH: A|= (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{− π/6}^{π/6}\cos^{2} (3θ)dθ; = (1)/(4)∫_{− π/6}^{π/6}(1 + \cos (6θ))dθ; = (1)/(4)(θ|_{− π/6}^{π/6} + (1)/(6)\sin (6θ)|_{− π/6}^{π/6}); = (1)/(4)(((π)/(6) − (− (π)/(6))) + (1)/(6)(\sin π − \sin (− π))); = (1)/(4)((π)/(3) + 0); = (π)/(12).]

Item 11 — Tutorial: Intuition Behind the Formula

Content:
We've been using the following formula for the area of the region bounded by a polar curve [MATH: r=r(\theta)] and the rays [MATH: \theta=\theta_1] and [MATH: \theta=\theta_2{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta]

Content:
But where does this formula come from?

Content:
To see where the formula comes from, we can think about breaking up the area bounded by a polar curve into infinitesimally small sectors of circles.

Content:
As shown in the graph below, each sector has a radius of [MATH: r] and spans an infinitesimally small angle, [MATH: \textrm d \theta.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f54818e0e1def6c498e34fd18ddf6925]

Content:
The ratio of the area of a sector to the full area of the circle must be the same as the ratio of the angle of the sector to a full revolution of the circle. So, if the area of a sector is [MATH: \textrm dA,] then we can set up and solve the following proportion:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\pi r^2} = \dfrac{\textrm d\theta}{2\pi} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \textrm dA = \dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \textrm d\theta]

Content:
Finally, to find the area under the curve, we can integrate the areas of all the sectors:

Content:
[MATH: A|= ∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}(1)/(2)r^{2}dθ; = (1)/(2)∫_{θ_{1}}^{θ_{2}}r^{2}dθ]
